_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol)**_

A non-homogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) retains independent increments but allows their distribution to depend on calendar time through a deterministic rate function \(\lambda(t)\).

Given \(\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(s)\,ds\), its key properties follow directly from the homogeneous case:

- \(N(s,t] \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\Lambda(t)-\Lambda(s))\).
- \(\mathbb E[N(s,t]]=\operatorname{Var}(N(s,t])=\Lambda(t)-\Lambda(s)\).
- The first-arrival survival function and density are
  \[
  \Pr(T_1>t)=e^{-\Lambda(t)},\qquad
  f_{T_1}(t)=\lambda(t)e^{-\Lambda(t)}.
  \]
- Interarrival times are generally neither i.i.d. nor exponential in physical time; exponential waiting times are special to constant \(\lambda\).
- The time-rescaled process \(\widetilde N(u)=N(\Lambda^{-1}(u))\), when \(\Lambda\) is invertible, is a unit-rate homogeneous Poisson process. Equivalently, \(\Lambda(T_n)\) are the arrival times of a unit-rate HPP.

So \(\Lambda(t)\), the cumulative intensity, replaces \(\lambda t\) everywhere in the homogeneous theory. The section’s first-arrival calculation is one instance of this broader time-change result.

_**User**_

Is the time-warping the easier way to get to these results?

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol)**_

Yes. Time-warping is usually the cleanest route.

Start with a unit-rate homogeneous Poisson process \(M(u)\), then define

\[
N(t) = M(\Lambda(t)),
\qquad
\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(r)\,\mathrm dr.
\]

All NHPP results follow immediately:

\[
N(s,t] = M(\Lambda(t))-M(\Lambda(s))
\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\Lambda(t)-\Lambda(s)).
\]

Independent increments are inherited because disjoint physical-time intervals map to disjoint intervals in warped time. Similarly, if \(S_n\) is the \(n\)th unit-rate HPP arrival, then

\[
T_n=\Lambda^{-1}(S_n).
\]

This makes clear why physical-time interarrival times are not generally exponential: the inverse warp depends on the current warped-time arrival location.

The infinitesimal-rate definition is still useful as a local characterization, but the time-change construction is generally the more direct way to derive distributions, simulate paths, and build intuition.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol)**_

The section currently jumps from the local definition to first-arrival time-warping, then to a “one-event Poisson process.” I would organize it around one central idea:

> An NHPP is an ordinary Poisson process running on a nonuniform clock.

Suggested structure:

### 1. Motivation: varying event frequency

Begin with the homogeneous result

\[
N(s,t]\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s)).
\]

Then explain that a time-dependent rate replaces elapsed time multiplied by \(\lambda\) with accumulated intensity

\[
\Lambda(s,t]=\int_s^t\lambda(r)\,dr.
\]

This immediately tells the reader what changes and what remains intact.

### 2. Definition and interpretation

Keep the infinitesimal definition, but explain

\[
\Pr(N(t,t+h]=1)=\lambda(t)h+o(h)
\]

as “the process currently runs at speed \(\lambda(t)\).” Then state the main result early:

\[
N(s,t]\sim\operatorname{Poisson}\!\left(\int_s^t\lambda(r)\,dr\right).
\]

Consequently,

\[
\mathbb E[N(s,t]]
=
\operatorname{Var}(N(s,t])
=
\int_s^t\lambda(r)\,dr.
\]

This count distribution is more fundamental than starting immediately with \(T_1\).

### 3. Time change

Introduce a unit-rate HPP \(M\) and construct

\[
N(t)=M(\Lambda(t)).
\]

This is more intuitive than beginning with the density transformation currently used around lines 261–269. It gives the increment law and independent increments almost for free.

Then explain the inverse relation for arrivals:

\[
T_n=\Lambda^{-1}(S_n),
\]

where \(S_n\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(n,1)\). In particular,

\[
\Lambda(T_n)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(n,1).
\]

The current first-arrival calculation becomes the \(n=1\) case rather than an isolated result.

### 4. Waiting-time consequences

Derive

\[
\Pr(T_1>t)=\Pr(N(t)=0)=e^{-\Lambda(t)}
\]

and hence

\[
f_{T_1}(t)=\lambda(t)e^{-\Lambda(t)}.
\]

More generally, conditional on no event between \(s\) and \(t\),

\[
\Pr(T_{\mathrm{next}}>t\mid T_{\mathrm{next}}>s)
=
\exp\left(-\int_s^t\lambda(r)\,dr\right).
\]

This makes the key contrast explicit: waiting times are exponential in cumulative-intensity time, but generally not in physical time.

### 5. Hazard-rate construction

Then introduce your desired-arrival-distribution construction:

\[
\lambda(t)=\frac{f(t)}{1-F(t)}.
\]

This now reads naturally as the converse: every sufficiently regular survival distribution can be represented as the first arrival of an NHPP.

Two technical qualifications should be stated:

- To guarantee \(T_1\leq1\), one needs
  \[
  \Lambda(t)\to\infty\quad\text{as }t\uparrow1,
  \]
  so the rate usually diverges near \(1\).
- An NHPP itself is not a “one-event process”; it continues producing events after the first. A process that stops after its first arrival is the NHPP stopped at \(T_1\).

### What I would cut or move

- The special case \(\lambda(t)=a g(t)\) repeats the general time-change calculation without adding much. Keep it only if \(a g(t)\) is needed later.
- Move the speculative discussion of joint distributions and Markov renewal processes at the end into a separate outlook section. It introduces substantially more machinery before the Poisson-process story has concluded.
- State assumptions when using \(\Lambda^{-1}\): strict monotonicity requires \(\lambda(t)>0\). With zero-rate intervals, use a generalized inverse.

That sequence gives both intuition and depth:

\[
\text{local rate}
\longrightarrow
\text{cumulative intensity}
\longrightarrow
\text{time change}
\longrightarrow
\text{counts and arrivals}
\longrightarrow
\text{hazard construction}.
\]
